title: Dynamic edge coloring with sublinear additive slack
formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic edge-coloring algorithm and fixed constants \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(C\ge1\), and \(a,b\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge2\), every fixed degree bound \(1\le\Delta\le n-1\), and every valid oblivious sequence of edge insertions and deletions, it explicitly maintains a proper coloring with at most
\[K(n,\Delta)=\Delta+\left\lceil C\Delta^{1-\gamma}(\log_2(n+2))^a\right\rceil\]
colors in expected amortized update time at most \(C(\log_2(n+2))^b\)? The algorithm must always return a valid coloring. The bound must hold uniformly in both \(n\) and \(\Delta\), with the same constants, not only at each fixed \(\Delta\).

This is the update-time question in the workshop report, with the polylogarithmic factors and probability/cost convention made explicit. The author's separate, weaker recourse-only question is context rather than the main target.
why: The question asks whether a changing graph can stay close to the optimal edge-color bound while each update costs only a polylogarithm. Its central issue is the joint dependence on graph size and degree: bounds that are fast for fixed relative error can become slow when the allowed extra colors shrink by a power of the degree. A resolution would sharpen the resource tradeoff for dynamic conflict-free scheduling represented by edge coloring.
status_note: The November 2024 report, Costa’s undated expanded primary note, Sadeh–Kaplan arXiv:2602.09497v2 (Theorems 2.5 and 2.8 and Section 3), and the publisher abstract for Christiansen’s SODA 2026 paper were checked on 2026-09-14. The recourse results retain restrictions on the palette or arboricity, and the deterministic result has a subpolynomial update bound rather than the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. A bounded search through the review date located no matching all-graph resolution. Source-open status records these verification limits, not an independent proof check of every cited result.

sentences: A changing graph must keep a proper integer color on every edge.
The target allows only a power-sublinear additive number of colors above the maximum-degree bound, up to logarithmic factors.
One uniform algorithm should maintain that coloring in polylogarithmic expected amortized time over all degree scales.
The question remains meaningful even when updates are chosen independently of the algorithm’s randomness.
Small recoloring counts and recent restricted-graph or subpolynomial-time results do not by themselves meet the stated total-work guarantee.

definitions:
The graph is undirected, simple and unweighted, on a fixed vertex set \([n]\), and starts without edges. Every insertion adds a currently absent edge between distinct vertices, and every deletion removes a currently present edge. The sequence may contain both operations in arbitrary order, always respecting maximum degree at most the input bound \(\Delta\). This is a fixed upper bound for the whole sequence, rather than the current degree recomputed after each update. Disconnected graphs are allowed; no sparsity or bipartiteness promise is imposed.

A proper edge coloring is a map \(\chi:E\to[K(n,\Delta)]\) in which distinct incident edges have distinct colors. The palette consists of fixed integer labels throughout the execution. Explicit maintenance requires storing the current integer color with every existing edge; each change to such a stored label is charged. Given a handle to an existing edge record, its color is available in constant time. Updates use endpoint labels, and locating or creating the record is part of their cost. The algorithm need not print all edge colors after each update.

Use a word-RAM with \(w=\lceil c_w\log_2(n+2)\rceil\)-bit words for a fixed algorithm-dependent constant \(c_w\), large enough for its polynomial space addresses and color labels. Charge one step for a word read/write, comparison, branch, Boolean operation, shift, modular addition/subtraction/multiplication, quotient/remainder by a nonzero word, or independent uniform random word. Only polynomially many persistent words are allowed, with one fixed exponent independent of the update horizon. The algorithm has a single finite program for all \(n,\Delta\); there is no uncharged input-dependent advice or table.

Initialization on the empty graph takes at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^b\) expected time. For every finite valid update sequence of length \(T\), the expected sum of all update work must be at most \(C T(\log_2(n+2))^b\). This includes writing colors, recolorings, lookup, memory management and any rebuilds. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices and is not revealed in advance. It may be arbitrarily long. Expectations are over the internal randomness; the constants are independent of \(n,\Delta,T\) and the sequence. Larger constants may absorb finite exceptional small instances.

Always-correct randomized behavior means that every completed update gives a proper coloring in the stated palette, and every finite valid execution terminates with probability one. No failure probability for an invalid coloring is allowed. Amortization permits expensive individual updates subject to every-prefix expected total bounds. Deterministic algorithms also qualify. The recourse is the number of existing edges whose colors change while processing an update; it is a lower bound on explicit update work, but bounding recourse does not bound the computation needed to select those changes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of such an algorithm and fixed constants. Any fixed positive \(\gamma<1\) suffices for a positive answer; an exponent that tends to zero with \(n\) does not. The time bound must be independent of polynomial factors in \(\Delta\), and every permitted graph and degree scale must be covered. A guarantee only on the number of recolorings, only on forests or bounded-arboricity graphs, or only for constant maximum degree is insufficient. A lower bound for repairing one adversarially prescribed starting coloring alone is insufficient to rule out an algorithm that controls the colorings it maintains.

context_blocks.text: The workshop report asks for a power saving in the additive number of colors together with polylogarithmic update time. The constants in the displayed target spell out its two suppressed polylogarithmic factors.

Costa’s expanded note explicitly separates recoloring cost from computation and says that even its recourse-only version is open against an oblivious adversary with amortization. This card retains the report’s stronger total-update-work target while choosing that permissive adversary and amortization setting.

Known algorithms use \((1+\varepsilon)\Delta\) colors with update bounds polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), up to polylogarithmic factors. Substituting an inverse-polynomial-in-degree relative slack can therefore introduce a polynomial degree dependence in time, which the target forbids.

The May 2026 Sadeh–Kaplan revision gives recourse improvements for large palettes and for graphs of low arboricity, where arboricity is the minimum number of forests covering all edges. Those restrictions and the distinction between recourse and running time remain essential; they do not establish the all-graph update-time target.

The SODA 2026 deterministic algorithm uses a relative-error palette and achieves subpolynomial update time in its stated accuracy range. Subpolynomial time is a larger class of bounds than polylogarithmic time, so this result does not itself provide the required guarantee.
